claims.text: Phase-selective recrystallization can simultaneously improve strength and ductility in a eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a duplex microstructure.
The starting duplex microstructure is in the as-cast state.
Weak phase boundaries and grain boundaries of the hard phase limit ductility.
Deformation followed by an optimized annealing schedule can trigger phase-selective recrystallization.
The treatment fully recrystallizes the soft phase while retaining a skeletal hard-phase network.
The treatment must be applied after deformation using composition-specific temperature-time profiles.
Manipulating strain partitioning between the soft and hard phases is associated with formation of the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure.
The resulting structural mediator is a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in a retained hard-phase skeleton.
The eliminated weak boundaries are locations where cracking typically initiates.
Eliminating weak boundaries and manipulating strain partitioning fully releases the strain-hardening capacity of the duplex phases.
The phase-selectively recrystallized alloy can attain approximately 2 GPa true tensile stress.
The phase-selectively recrystallized alloy can attain approximately 35% uniform elongation.
Both strength and uniform elongation will be higher than in the untreated as-cast alloy.
Departures from the required temperature, time, or deformation pretreatment may prevent simultaneous strength and ductility enhancement.
The intervention may not work for compositions with substantially different phase stability.
The optimal processing window and recrystallization kinetics vary with alloy composition.
Minor phase variations may affect recrystallization behavior.

contradictions.description: The control is described as remaining in the as-cast state, but the experiment also instructs that the two sets have identical deformation pretreatments. A deformation-pretreated control would no longer be a strictly as-cast baseline.
